trajectory.position_description: He settles into adult communion through marriage, family life, and philanthropic usefulness. His identity is no longer organized around proving himself or escaping constraint, but around sustaining others.

relational_axes.axis_name: From neighboring outsider to quasi-family member
relational_axes.pole_start: Starts as a curious neighbor and occasional visitor who longs for the warmth he sees from outside.
relational_axes.pole_end: Ends as an integrated family member in all but name, trusted in crises, welcomed in rituals, and included in the household's emotional and practical life.

trajectory.position_description: The Marches are initially a source of fascination and emotional hunger. He watches them, receives their kindness indirectly, and begins to want entry into their world.
Through gifts, rescues, shared games, and crisis support, he becomes a regular and valued presence in the household.
His marriage to Amy completes his transition from guest to kin. He is now part of the family not by proximity alone but by permanent relational membership.

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Laurie’s arc with the March family is one of progressive belonging. He moves from longing at the threshold to full participation in their domestic and emotional life.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: Laurie’s arc in Little Women is strongly grounded in scholarship on his movement from outsider-neighbor to intimate quasi-son/brother within the March household. Critics repeatedly note that his social and emotional incorporation into the family is central to the novel’s domestic structure, even as the text preserves his status as “not quite” kin by blood or marriage. The axis is therefore well supported by published criticism on domesticity, kinship, and the March/Laurie relationship.
